pages.name: A rate in proportion
pages.text: A capacitor `C`, charged to 12 V, discharges through a resistor `R`. The current leaving it is `v ÷ R`. You know `i = C dv/dt`. That current drains it, so `C dv/dt = −v ÷ R`. The rule is `dv/dt = −v ÷ RC`. Here `RC` is 20 kΩ × 100 µF, which is 2 s. At 12 V the voltage falls 6 V a second. At 6 V it falls 3 V a second. The rate is [[in proportion to what is left]].

Rate arrows at 12 volts and 6 volts. The arrow at 6 volts is half as steep in volts a second.

pages.name: The rate at 3 V
pages.task: The voltage has fallen to 3 V. What is its rate there, in V a second?
pages.why: The rule takes the voltage over `RC`, with a minus sign. So the rate is −3 ÷ 2 = −1.5 V a second. The voltage still falls, but more gently than at 12 V.

pages.name: Equal times, equal fractions
pages.text: A window 1 s wide slides along the curve. Its start and end voltages both fall as it goes. Yet end ÷ start stays at 0.607. From 12 V it ends at 7.28 V. From 2.68 V it ends at 1.62 V. The rate is always the same share of the voltage. So each second keeps the same share. Under growth, `dy/dt = +y ÷ 2`, each second multiplies by 1.649 instead. That is `e^(1/2)`, so every 2 s multiplies by e.

pages.name: Separate the variables
pages.text: To find the curve, [[separate the variables]]. Divide both sides of the rule by `v`. That gives `(1 ÷ v) dv/dt = −1 ÷ RC`. Now integrate both sides over `t`. The short way to write this is `dv ÷ v = −dt ÷ RC`. Every `v` is on the left and every `t` on the right. It does not mean cancelling the d's. Not every rule splits like this, but this one does.

pages.name: Separate a decay rule
pages.task: Radioactive atoms follow `dN/dt = −λN`. Here `N` is the number left and `λ` is the decay constant. Which line separates it?
pages.why: Divide both sides by `N`. Every `N` is then on the left, with `dN`. Only `dt` is on the right, with the constant `−λ`. That gives `dN ÷ N = −λ dt`.

pages.name: Integrate both sides
pages.text: Now integrate both sides. For a positive `v`, the slope of `ln v` is `1 ÷ v`. So the left side gives `ln v`. The right side gives `−t ÷ RC`. Their two constants join into one `+ c`. Raise e to each side to undo the ln. That gives `v = e^(−t/RC + c)`, which splits into `e^(c) × e^(−t/RC)`. Call `e^(c)` by one letter, `A`. At `t = 0` the curve is at `A`, so `A` is the start. The start at 12 V picks `v = 12 e^(−t/2)`.
pages.alt: Rule: d v by d t equals minus v divided by RC. RC equals 2 s. v equals 12 e to the power minus t/2. Curves for starts of 3, 6, 9 and 12 volts, all with the same time constant.

pages.name: Pick the curve
pages.task: Call `RC` the time constant, `τ`. Which curve starts at 9 V with `τ = 3 s`?
pages.why: At `t = 0` the curve must be at 9 V, so `A = 9`. The power is `−t ÷ τ`, which is `−t/3`. So `v = 9 e^(−t/3)`. After one `τ` it is down to 0.368 of its start.

pages.name: Put it back
pages.text: Now put the answer back into the rule. A rider slides along `v = 12 e^(−t/2)`. It carries two numbers. One is the curve's own slope there. The other is what the rule asks for, `−v ÷ 2`. They agree everywhere. At 2 s both read −2.21 V a second. The slope of `e^(kt)` is `k` times `e^(kt)`. Here `k` is `−1 ÷ 2`. So the slope is `−v ÷ 2` at every `t`, which is the rule. Wherever the rider sits, the two numbers match.

pages.task: A coil of 0.5 H carries 2.4 A. Its supply is taken away. The current dies round a loop through 10 Ω. What is the current after 0.05 s?
pages.why: For a coil the time constant is `L ÷ R`, so 0.5 ÷ 10 = 0.05 s. That makes 0.05 s exactly one `τ`. One `τ` keeps 0.368 of the start. 2.4 × 0.368 = 0.883 A.

pages.name: Growth over one τ
pages.task: A growth rule, `dy/dt = +y ÷ 5`, starts from 100. What is `y` after 5 s?
pages.why: Here `τ` is 5 s and the sign is plus. So 5 s is one `τ`, and each `τ` multiplies by e. After 5 s, `y` is 100 × e, about 272. The rate grows as `y` grows. A reactor's power grows this way. Its period is the time the power takes to change by a factor of e.
